claims.statement: `app/src/main/search/client.ts` is the repository's only production client of Listary's local HTTP API — its `listarySearch` is the single I/O entry point and it is imported only by `services/search.ts` — while every other export (the constants, `Debouncer`, `buildRequest`, `parseResponse`, `classifyFailure`, `backoffDelay` in `search/engine.ts`) is dependency-free pure logic that imports nothing but a type, so the whole link except its transport is offline-testable.

The engine's wire contract is `POST /api/v1/search` on the loopback host `BASE_HOST = '127.0.0.1'` and port `BASE_PORT = 38431`, with `Content-Type: application/json`, `Content-Length` and `Connection: close`, and a JSON body of `query`, `limit` and `offset`; a success is an `ok` flag plus `data.results[]` rows (upstream `path`, `name`, `type`, `size_bytes`, `modified_at`, `score`) and `data.total`, and the only error codes the client knows are `SEARCH_UNAVAILABLE` and `TOO_MANY_REQUESTS`.

`buildRequest` emits only `query`, `limit` and `offset`, so the integration never uses the optional `search_in`, `types` or `extensions` filters declared by Listary's in-app API dialog — results are not scoped to a directory, restricted to folders, or filtered by extension — and the dialog's default `limit` of 10 with a ceiling of 100 is not what the client sends: it sends `DEFAULT_LIMIT = 8`, while `offset` is only a pass-through that the service always calls with 0.

`parseResponse` reads only `data.results` and `data.total` (ignoring `data.query`, `data.offset`, `data.limit` and `data.count`), coerces each row into a `SearchResultItem` with stringified fields and `''`/`0`/`'file'` defaults, skips rows that are not objects, treats a missing, null or non-object `data` as an ok model with `total=0` and no items, and deliberately does not enforce `limit` locally — twelve rows for `limit=8` remain twelve, with truncation left to the renderer's `SEARCH_LIMIT = 8` slice.

`parseResponse` ignores the `ok` flag and inspects only `data`, so an error payload such as `{"ok": false, "error": "TOO_MANY_REQUESTS"}` parses into an ordinary empty success model; a caller must run `classifyFailure` first or it will present a throttled or failing engine as `NO RESULTS` / `TOTAL 0`, which is why `SearchService.onPayload` classifies before it parses.

`classifyFailure` is the single decision point mapping failures to three kinds: an `ok` payload gives `null`; a `ListaryNetworkError` or an error payload whose string is `SEARCH_UNAVAILABLE` gives `offline`; `TOO_MANY_REQUESTS` gives `rate_limited`; and every other error code or thrown value — including the `SyntaxError` the client rejects a non-JSON body with — gives `error`.

`offline` is deliberately narrow — transport failure plus the explicit `SEARCH_UNAVAILABLE` code only — so that a reachable but misbehaving engine (invalid JSON, unknown error code) is classified `error`: it never shows the `ENGINE OFFLINE` badge, never schedules an automatic retry, and waits for the next input instead, because an online-but-broken engine must not masquerade as an absent one.

Because Listary's API has no keep-alive, `listarySearch` builds a fresh request with `agent: false` and `Connection: close` on every call, reads the whole response body, and passes `HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS = 3000` as the connect/read timeout; there is no connection pool, production never overrides the timeout, and the per-call `ListaryEndpoint.timeoutMs` field exists so tests can use a short one.

`listarySearch` never inspects the HTTP status code: the response chunks are concatenated, decoded as `utf8` and passed to `JSON.parse`, a non-JSON body rejects with a plain `SyntaxError` that is classified `error` rather than `offline`, and valid JSON that is not an object is handed to the caller unchanged instead of being treated as an empty result.

The API's loopback-only listener on `127.0.0.1` with no CORS support makes a main-process client the only structurally possible caller — a browser context or the panel's renderer page could never reach the endpoint — which is why the query leaves the process as a loopback POST and no write endpoint was added for search; ADR-0003's related conclusion that the search panel had to be a service-owned native window was superseded by ADR-0004, which moved the search surface into the panel's own HTML overlay while keeping the caller-side constraint.

Retry arithmetic lives in the engine while retry policy lives in the service: `backoffDelay(attempt) = min(500 * 2 ** (attempt - 1), MAX_BACKOFF_MS)` with `MAX_BACKOFF_MS = 5000` yields `500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 5000, 5000, …` milliseconds and `OFFLINE_RETRY_MS = 3000` is the flat offline cadence, while the service owns the attempt counter and the single pending-retry deadline, resolved by its 50 ms pump, and re-sends through `Debouncer.feedDue` so a retry bypasses the debounce window and clears same-word dedup.

`config.search.port` is the only endpoint override: it is validated as an integer in `1..65535` with `BASE_PORT = 38431` as the default (a non-integer or out-of-range value warns and falls back), reaches the kernel at assembly as `search: { port }`, and is captured when `SearchService` is constructed, so changing it requires restarting the panel; pointing it at a dead port is how the acceptance battery reproduces the offline engine path on a machine where Listary is running, producing the `ENGINE OFFLINE` badge and a recorded 3 s silent retry.

The unit tests keep the real API out of the process but not the transport: `tests/search/engine.spec.ts` asserts the pure layer (debounce window, request construction with `offset`, response parsing, the classification table, the backoff curve), while `tests/search/client.spec.ts` starts a `node:http` fake API on `127.0.0.1` and runs the real client against it — offset body, empty and error payloads, connection refused, a forced 120 ms timeout, a non-JSON body, and the no-keep-alive behaviour — so the wire layer is covered in-process, and no test ever contacts the real Listary engine.

The historical source of the contract is Listary 7's in-app `Options → HTTP API` dialog, transcribed into `.scratch/listary-search/spec.md`, which `engine.ts` still cites as its contract reference; the discovery probes behind that transcription read only structural configuration (truncating any long value to a length plus a four-character prefix, never reading license or history data, and never storing a value long enough to be one) and Listary-owned listening sockets, and confirm the live endpoint by posting benign queries and printing `ok`, `data.total`, `data.count` and per-item `type`/`name`/`score`/`path`.

Listary 7 is beta and the port and response shape may change in a release, and nothing in this repository detects that at load time — a moved port degrades into `offline`, while renamed response fields degrade silently into defaulted or empty results; the implemented acceptance battery's own independent direct probe (`engineProbeFirst`, a second implementation of the request body that only passes when the freshly created probe file ranks first in `data.results`) is the practical detector.

The V6 route to query prefilling was ruled out before this integration was chosen: V6's `-search` command line opens a window with the query unfilled and V6 exposes no API at all, which is why the V7 local HTTP API is the only supported integration surface rather than just the newest one.

`ListaryNetworkError` is the transport-failure normalisation for the whole link: the client wraps every socket error (using `err.code` when present and the message otherwise) and its own timeout into that class, and `classifyFailure` keys `offline` on the class rather than re-inspecting Node error codes at each call site, so every other thrown value is `error`.

`SearchResultItem` is the integration boundary's data model: `parseResponse` maps the API's `snake_case` row fields into the camel-case `SearchResultItem` declared in the shared bridge contract, and that model is what crosses to the renderer in the `search/results` payload of `total` plus `items`, so a field change in either direction has to be made in both the parser and the contract type.

A source-level guard in `tests/contract.spec.ts` pins the loopback target to the engine constants and keeps query text out of storage: the three search files may not reference the usage log, may not call `writeFileSync` or `appendFileSync`, may not contain a hard-coded `http(s)://` URL, and `client.ts` must reference `BASE_HOST`.

`ERR_UNAVAILABLE` and `ERR_RATE_LIMITED` in `engine.ts` are wire-level identifiers rather than display strings: `classifyFailure` compares the payload's `error` against them, so renaming a constant silently reclassifies that engine answer into `error` even though the server's output is unchanged.
